results.summary: This is a simple parity generator that takes 8 input bits and produces a parity output on 4 output pins. It is implemented as a Wokwi learning exercise, likely using basic logic gates. The design is tested by setting input switches and observing the output LEDs. The documentation is minimal and does not specify the exact parity function or output encoding.

This design displays the characters 'CIt' on a 7-segment display using a D flip-flop ring counter. It is implemented in Wokwi and has a 1 Hz clock. The inputs include a run signal and four state initialization bits, while the outputs drive the seven segments plus an eighth segment. The documentation is brief and does not provide a schematic or detailed explanation of the state machine.

This project implements a 4-bit full adder and subtractor with an externally triggered hardware trojan inserted in the critical path. It includes LFSR outputs and inputs, and displays results on a 7-segment display. Testing requires DIP switches, an external trigger signal, and a pattern generator and logic analyzer. The design is notable for demonstrating a hardware trojan in a simple arithmetic circuit.

This design implements an even and odd BCD counter that can be selected via two inputs. When input 1 is high, the even counter is active; when input 2 is high, the odd counter is active. The outputs are 7-bit BCD values intended to drive a 7-segment display. Testing involves setting the inputs and observing the count on a connected 7-segment display.

This project aims to create a modern take on 74-series universal gate chips, eventually becoming a Wokwi port of unigate-gf. It provides various logic functions through configurable inputs and bidirectional pins. The design is tested by running a testbench in the test directory. The documentation is sparse and does not detail the exact functionality or pin mappings.

This design controls the direction of a DC motor using logic gates, with inputs and outputs mapped to specific pins. It is implemented in Wokwi and includes a schematic link. The documentation is in Spanish and describes the logic for changing rotation direction, but it is somewhat disorganized and includes irrelevant information about an LFSR. Testing requires external hardware such as a motor driver and motor.

This project implements a 32-bit Fibonacci LFSR or PRNG, as suggested by the title and description. It has two inputs and eight outputs, but the documentation is essentially absent, providing no details on functionality or testing. The design is likely a sequence generator based on the Fibonacci series. Without further documentation, the exact behavior and usage cannot be determined.

This design generates a 50 Hz PWM signal for testing RC servos, with the pulse width controlled by an 8-bit input. It uses a 10 MHz clock to create the timing and outputs the servo pulse on a bidirectional pin. The position is also indicated on a 7-segment display. Testing requires an RC servo connected to the output pin.

This design reads three digital encoders, debounces the inputs, and outputs three PWM signals to control RGB LED brightness. It is a Zero to ASIC demo project implemented in Verilog. Testing involves twisting each encoder and observing the brightness change on connected LEDs. External hardware includes three digital encoders and an RGB LED.

This chip decodes the QOA audio format, a simple lossy compression for 16-bit PCM audio, via an SPI slave interface. It acts as a co-processor, requiring an external microcontroller to handle file I/O and streaming. The design has been tested in silicon and works, achieving up to 176,056 samples per second. Notable for its compact implementation and potential for real-time audio streaming.
